implementation_notes: Scala makes the pattern checkable: scala.annotation.tailrec is a standard annotation whose documentation says the compiler verifies that the annotated method will be compiled with tail-call optimization and issues an error if it cannot be optimized into a loop. The recursive formulation therefore stays in the source while the bytecode is a loop, and the failure mode of a lost tail call is a compile error rather than a latent overflow. The optimization covers self-recursive calls; for mutual recursion Scala supplies scala.util.control.TailCalls, whose methods implement tail calls via trampolining.
pitfalls: @tailrec only proves self-recursion: a mutually recursive pair (isEven/isOdd) fails the annotation and needs TailCalls.trampoline instead.
A call inside try/catch or whose result is used afterwards (a + gcd(...)) is not a tail call, and the annotation turns that into a compile error - which is the feature, but it forces restructuring.
TailCalls bounds the stack by allocating a heap frame per step, so it is a correctness tool for mutual recursion, not a free replacement for a loop.
